'''Energy Star<!--lowercase per WP:MOSTM-->''' (trademarked '''ENERGY STAR''') is a voluntary U.S. government [[Efficient energy use|energy-efficiency]] program established by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|U.S. Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENERGY STAR Impacts {{!}} ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/impacts |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261010123041/https://www.energystar.gov/about/impacts |archive-date=2026-10-10 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.energystar.gov |language=en |quote=The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency launched the ENERGY STAR program in 1992.}}</ref> 

The program is jointly administered by the EPA and the [[United States Department of Energy|U.S. Department of Energy]] (DOE).<ref>{{Cite web |title=How ENERGY STAR Works {{!}} ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/how-energy-star-works |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261010125407/https://www.energystar.gov/about/how-energy-star-works |archive-date=2026-10-10 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.energystar.gov |language=en |quote="The ENERGY STAR Program is administered jointly by U.S. Department of ENERGY (DOE) and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)."}}</ref> In March 2026, the DOE was designated the lead federal agency, with the transfer of program responsibilities targeted for completion by July 2027.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-10-10 |title=ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/energy-star |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261010130542/https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/energy-star |archive-date=2026-10-10 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=Energy.gov |language=en |quote="Leadership of ENERGY STAR is currently transitioning from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to the U.S. Department of Energy. Read the Memorandum of Agreement and Transition Plan."}}</ref> 

Energy Star establishes energy efficiency specifications, and those that meet these specifications are eligible to display the Energy Star logo.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How ENERGY STAR Works | url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/how-energy-star-works | access-date=2026-10-10 | website=www.energystar.gov | language=en | quote="ENERGY STAR is a voluntary labeling program authorized by Section 131 of the Energy Policy Act of 2025, as amended. 42 U.S.C. § 6249a. The government sets energy efficiency specifications and those that meet them can choose to display the ENERGY STAR logo. In turn, consumers and businesses who want to save energy and money can look for the ENERGY STAR label when making buying decisions."}}</ref> More than 75 product categories are eligible for the Energy Star label, including appliances, electronics, lighting, heating and cooling systems, and commercial equipment such as food service products.<ref>{{Cite web | date=2024-02-02 | title=What Makes a Product ENERGY STAR Certified? {{!}} ENERGY STAR | url=https://www.energystar.gov/products/ask-the-experts/what-makes-product-energy-star-certified | access-date=2024-10-28 | website=www.energystar.gov | language=en | quote="Products must achieve high levels of energy efficiency set by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in order to earn the ENERGY STAR label. Over 75 types of products can earn the label, in categories such as appliances, electronics, lighting, heating and cooling, and commercial products such as food service equipment. In order to receive certification, products must undergo a three-step process."}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Energy Efficient Products {{!}} ENERGY STAR | url=https://www.energystar.gov/products | access-date=2024-10-28 | website=www.energystar.gov | language=en}}</ref> In the United States, the Energy Star label often appears with the [[EnergyGuide]] label of eligible appliances to highlight energy-efficient products and compare energy use and operating costs.<ref>{{Cite web | date=2024-02-02 | title=What's the Difference Between the Energy Guide and ENERGY STAR? {{!}} ENERGY STAR | url=https://www.energystar.gov/products/ask-the-experts/whats-difference-between-energy-guide-and-energy-star | access-date=2024-10-28 | website=www.energystar.gov | language=en | quote="Both the EnergyGuide and the ENERGY STAR labels are intended to help you make smart energy choices. Used in conjunction, these labels can help you choose which product is right for you. The ENERGY STAR label will help you easily identify which products are the most efficient options, and then the EnergyGuide can be used to directly compare your top choices and give you an estimate of the energy use and operating cost. Saving energy is good for your wallet and good for the climate."}}</ref>

One of the most successful voluntary initiatives introduced by the U.S. government, the program has saved 5 trillion kilowatt-hours of electricity, more than [[US$]]500 billion in energy costs, and prevented 4 billion metric tons of [[greenhouse gas emissions]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web | title=ENERGY STAR Impacts {{!}} ENERGY STAR | url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/impacts | access-date=2024-10-28 | website=www.energystar.gov | language=en | quote="The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency launched the ENERGY STAR program in 1992. Since then, ENERGY STAR has grown to become the international standard for energy efficiency and one of the most successful voluntary U.S. government programs in history ..."}}</ref>

According to the EPA, more than 790,000 Americans were employed in manufacturing or installing Energy Star-certified products, based on employment estimates from the 2024 U.S. Energy and Employment Report.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://energy.gov/downloads/2017-us-energy-and-employment-report |title=2017 U.S. Energy and Employment Report {{!}} Department of Energy |website=energy.gov |access-date=2017-11-14 |archive-date=2021-01-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210103010311/https://www.energy.gov/downloads/2017-us-energy-and-employment-report |url-status=live}}</ref> The 2026 report separately estimated that approximately 344,000 Americans worked in the broader energy-efficiency manufacturing sector in 2025.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.energy.gov/documents/2026-useer-appendices-i |title=2026 United States Energy & Employment Report: Appendices A–I |date= |year=2026 |publisher=U.S. Department of Energy |at=Appendix F, p. 67, Figure F-2 |quote="Of the 2,969,000 jobs found in relevant energy manufacturing subsectors in 2025 — such as lighting, household appliances or HVAC equipment manufacturing — about 344,000 workers manufactured energy-efficient products as defined in these appendices." |access-date=2026-10-11}}</ref>

Outside the United States, elements of the Energy Star program are implemented in Canada, Japan, and Switzerland.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web | title=ENERGY STAR International Partners {{!}} ENERGY STAR | url=https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/international-partners | access-date=2024-10-28 | website=www.energystar.gov | language=en}}</ref> Previous international agreements, including those with the European Union and the European Free Trade Association, have expired.<ref>{{Cite web | title=EU Energy Star | url=https://ec.europa.eu/energy/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-products/energy-star_en | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210211081256/https://ec.europa.eu/energy/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-products/energy-star_en | archive-date=2021-02-11 | access-date=2021-02-10}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

==History==

=== Establishment and early expansion (1992-2005) ===
The Energy Star program was established by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]] in 1992 under Section 103(g) of the [[Clean Air Act (United States)|Clean Air Act]] (42 U.S.C. § 7403(g)).<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENERGY STAR Program |url=https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF10753 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.congress.gov |quote="EPA established ENERGY STAR in 1992 under the authority of the Clean Air Act, Section 103(g)."}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first= |date= |title=Clean Air Act Title I - Air Pollution Prevention and Control, Parts A through D |url=https://www.epa.gov/clean-air-act-overview/clean-air-act-title-i-air-pollution-prevention-and-control-parts-through-d |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260424015448/https://www.epa.gov/clean-air-act-overview/clean-air-act-title-i-air-pollution-prevention-and-control-parts-through-d |archive-date=2026-04-24 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/USCODE-2010-title42/pdf/USCODE-2010-title42-chap85-subchapI-partA-sec7403.pdf|title=Section 103(g) of the Clean Air Act|last=U.S. General Publishing Office|access-date=2017-10-25|archive-date=2018-08-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180815012217/https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/USCODE-2010-title42/pdf/USCODE-2010-title42-chap85-subchapI-partA-sec7403.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Initially a voluntary labeling initiative to promote energy-efficient products and help consumers identify them, the program first covered [[Computer|computers]] and [[Display device|displays]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our History {{!}} ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/how-energy-star-works/history |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261010200223/https://www.energystar.gov/about/how-energy-star-works/history |archive-date=2026-10-10 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.energystar.gov |language=en |quote="1992 EPA launch of the ENERGY STAR label for office products starting with computers and displays."}}</ref> It has since expanded to include more than 75 product categories, as well as energy-efficient homes, commercial buildings, and industrial facilities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENERGY STAR Product Specification Development Efforts {{!}} ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/products_partner_resources/brand-owner/spec-dev-efforts |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.energystar.gov |language=en |quote="Since its creation in 1992, the ENERGY STAR program has grown to designate energy efficient products in more than 75 categories, all of which are independently certified."}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/tools/Ingredient_Brand_Guide.pdf |title=ENERGY STAR Products Ingredient Brand Guide |date= |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |page=9 |access-date=2026-10-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261010201741/https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/tools/Ingredient_Brand_Guide.pdf |archive-date=2026-10-10 |format=PDF}}</ref>

As part of the program's early expansion, the EPA and the [[United States Department of Energy|DOE]] signed a memorandum of cooperation in 1996 to coordinate efforts and expand the program's scope.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-106shrg59418/pdf/CHRG-106shrg59418.pdf#page=70 |title=Global Climate Change: Joint Hearing Before The Subcommittee On Energy Research, Development, Production And Regulation |author= |date=1999-05-20 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |publication-date=1999 |pages=64–66 |access-date=2026-10-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729035145/https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-106shrg59418/pdf/CHRG-106shrg59418.pdf |archive-date=2026-07-29 |format=PDF |url-status=live |work= |series=S. Hrg. 106-227}}</ref>

In 2000, the [[Consortium for Energy Efficiency|Consortium for Energy Efficiency (CEE)]] began conducting national household surveys to measure consumer awareness and understanding of the ENERGY STAR label and its influence on purchasing decisions.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.energystar.gov/ia/partners/publications/pubdocs/2000%20ES_Survey_rep.pdf |title=CEE ENERGY STAR Household Survey Report (2000): Part I – Results |author= |date=2001-02-09 |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |at=Executive Summary and Section 1.2 |quote="In the summer/fall of 2000, The Consortium for Energy Efficiency (CEE) sponsored a national household mail survey to ascertain consumer awareness and understanding of the ENERGY STAR label as well as its influence on energy-related purchasing decisions." |access-date=2026-10-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261010203911/https://www.energystar.gov/ia/partners/publications/pubdocs/2000%20ES_Survey_rep.pdf |archive-date=2026-10-10 |format=PDF}}</ref><ref name="essurvey">{{cite web | url = http://www.cee1.org/content/household-energy-star-awareness-surveys | title = National Awareness of Energy Star | access-date = 2016-07-07 | work = Consortium for Energy Efficiency and US EPA | publisher = US EPA | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160725181354/http://www.cee1.org/content/household-energy-star-awareness-surveys | archive-date = 2016-07-25 | url-status = dead}}</ref> 

In 2005, Congress formally authorized Energy Star through Section 131 of the [[Energy Policy Act of 2005]], which added Section 324A to the [[Energy Policy and Conservation Act]] (42 U.S.C. § 6294a).<ref name=":3">{{cite web |date=2005-08-08 |title=Energy Policy Act of 2005 |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-109publ58/html/PLAW-109publ58.htm |access-date=2026-10-10 |publisher=U.S. Government Publishing Office |at=Section 131(a), 119 Stat. 620}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{cite web |date=2024 |title=42 U.S.C. § 6294a – Energy Star program |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title42/pdf/USCODE-2024-title42-chap77-subchapIII-partA-sec6294a.pdf |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=United States Code |publisher=U.S. Government Publishing Office |at=p. 6715, subsections (a)–(b) |format=PDF}}</ref> The provision established the voluntary program within both the EPA and the DOE and required that responsibilities be divided according to applicable agreements between them.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />

The EPA develops and manages Energy Star Portfolio Manager, an online energy tracking and benchmarking tool for commercial buildings. The DOE manages Home Performance with Energy Star and provides technical support, including test procedure development for products and some verification testing of products.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=partners.mou|title=EPA-DOE Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)|publisher=U.S. EPA|access-date=2017-10-25|archive-date=2020-07-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731011649/https://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=partners.mou|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Certification reforms (2009-2011) ===
Before 2011, Energy Star product qualification relied largely on manufacturers' self-reported data, a process that the [[United States Government Accountability Office|Government Accountability Office]] (GAO) found to be vulnerable to fraud and abuse.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2010-03-10 |title=Energy Star Program: Covert Testing Shows the Energy Star Program Certification Process Is Vulnerable to Fraud and Abuse {{!}} U.S. GAO |url=https://www.gao.gov/assets/files.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-470.pdf |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=U.S. Government Accountability Office |language=en |quote="GAO’s investigation shows that Energy Star is for the most part a self- certification program vulnerable to fraud and abuse. GAO obtained Energy Star certifications for 15 bogus products, including a gas-powered alarm clock."}}</ref> In September 2009, the EPA and DOE signed a memorandum of understanding to strengthen Energy Star product qualification and verification procedures, including testing before qualification and expanded verification testing of certified products.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/memorandum-understanding-improving-energy-efficiency-products-and-buildings |title=Memorandum of Understanding on Improving the Energy Efficiency of Products and Buildings |author= |date=2009-09-30 |publisher=U.S. Department of Energy |access-date=2026-10-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260703191642/https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/memorandum-understanding-improving-energy-efficiency-products-and-buildings |archive-date=2026-07-03 |format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-11-888.pdf |title=Energy Star: Providing Opportunities for Additional Review of EPA's Decisions Could Strengthen the Program |date=2011-09-30 |publisher=U.S. Government Accountability Office |pages=7–8 |id=GAO-11-888 |quote="Second, the MOU increases the amount of testing required to verify the performance of Energy Star-qualified products. Before the MOU, the program generally relied on a self-certification process for manufacturers to qualify products for the Energy Star label. Under the MOU, all products are now required to be tested in an accredited laboratory, and the results submitted to EPA before the products can be qualified for the Energy Star label. In addition, the MOU calls for increasing the amount of market- based testing used to verify that Energy Star-qualified products continue to meet program requirements. For this testing, selected products are taken off the shelf at retail locations and tested to determine whether they meet the Energy Star standards. The MOU also calls for the market- based testing to consist of a combination of EPA and DOE testing and manufacturer-funded testing administered by EPA or DOE, or testing by other third parties." |access-date=2026-10-11 |format=PDF}}</ref> 

Later in 2010, the EPA established new third-party certification procedures, which took effect on January 1, 2011. Under these procedures, products seeking Energy Star qualification were required to undergo testing by EPA-recognized laboratories and certification by EPA-recognized certification bodies.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-11-888.pdf |title=Energy Star: Providing Opportunities for Additional Review of EPA's Decisions Could Strengthen the Program |date=2011-09-30 |publisher=U.S. Government Accountability Office |id=GAO-11-888 |quote="EPA and DOE have made considerable progress in their ongoing efforts to implement significant changes to the Energy Star program agreed to in the 2009 MOU. These changes include expanding product qualification and verification testing, updating program requirements, and piloting a program to promote the most efficient Energy Star products. In 2010, EPA developed and instituted new third-party certification procedures to qualify products for the Energy Star label. The new procedures took effect on January 1, 2011." |access-date=2026-10-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260722155312/https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-11-888.pdf |archive-date=2026-07-22 |format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/asset/document/EPA_Cover_Letter.pdf |title=Revised ENERGY STAR Partner Commitments and Product Specifications Letter |date=2010-10-26 |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |access-date=2026-10-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260715233040/https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/asset/document/EPA_Cover_Letter.pdf |archive-date=2026-07-15 |format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Third-Party Certification |url=https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/products_partner_resources/third-party-cert |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260811210500/https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/products_partner_resources/third-party-cert |archive-date=2026-08-11 |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=ENERGY STAR |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref> Laboratories and certification bodies must meet EPA recognition requirements, including applicable accreditation and oversight criteria.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Certification Body Resources {{!}} ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/products_partner_resources/third-party-cert/cbs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260716010452/https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/products_partner_resources/third-party-cert/cbs |archive-date=2026-07-16 |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=www.energystar.gov |language=en |quote="EPA–recognized certification bodies (CBs) certify products that meet ENERGY STAR requirements and report information on those products to EPA. A CB must be EPA–recognized to certify products. One of the key criteria for recognition is accreditation to ISO/IEC 17065 by an accreditation body that is an International Accreditation Forum Multilateral Recognition Agreement (IAF MLA) signatory. CBs must verify that test results are from an EPA–recognized laboratory, maintain open correspondence with EPA, and cooperate with their AB for ongoing accreditation. CBs are also responsible for administering verification testing and challenge testing. CBs for insulation have unique requirements."}}</ref> In addition, a percentage of unique products  in each category undergo annual post-market verification testing to confirm continued compliance with specifications.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Verification Testing of Products {{!}} ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/products_partner_resources/brand-owner/verification-testing |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260716011737/https://www.energystar.gov/partner-resources/products_partner_resources/brand-owner/verification-testing |archive-date=2026-07-16 |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=www.energystar.gov |language=en |quote="ENERGY STAR certified products are subject to post-market verification testing administered by certification bodies. Consistent with EPA’s disqualification procedures, product models that fail verification testing are disqualified from using the ENERGY STAR label."}}</ref> The EPA currently oversees more than twenty recognized certification bodies and more than 700 recognized laboratories.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENERGY STAR Certification {{!}} ENERGY STAR |url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/how-energy-star-works/energy-star-certification |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260921205847/https://www.energystar.gov/about/how-energy-star-works/energy-star-certification |archive-date=2026-09-21 |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=www.energystar.gov |language=en |quote="EPA currently oversees third-party certification and manages certified product lists for tens of thousands of product models, including oversight of more than twenty certification bodies and more than 700 recognized labs. EPA also oversees post-market testing of a subset of all products each year to ensure product performance, as well as periodic audits of product labeling on shelves at major retailers to monitor use of the mark."}}</ref> In 2023, 1,218 certified Energy Star product models completed  verification testing, with an overall compliance rate of 94%.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/2024-04/2023%20ENERGY%20STAR%20Verification%20Testing%20Summary%20%28Web%20Version%29.pdf |title=ENERGY STAR Labeled Products: Verification Testing, 2023 Summary |date= |year=2024 |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |page=1 |access-date=2026-10-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260716002132/https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/2024-04/2023%20ENERGY%20STAR%20Verification%20Testing%20Summary%20(Web%20Version).pdf |archive-date=2026-07-16 |format=PDF}}</ref>

=== Funding disputes and administrative transition (2017-2026) ===
In March 2017, the Trump Administration proposed eliminating federal funding for the Energy Star program as part of its fiscal year 2018 budget.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BUDGET-2018-MSV/pdf/BUDGET-2018-MSV.pdf |title=Fiscal Year 2018 Budget: Major Savings and Reforms |date=2017 |publisher=Office of Management and Budget |page=85 |quote="The Budget eliminates funding for Energy Star and several other voluntary partnership programs related to energy and climate change." |access-date=2026-10-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260828010955/https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BUDGET-2018-MSV/pdf/BUDGET-2018-MSV.pdf |archive-date=2026-08-28 |format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2017-03-16 |title=Trump Budget Plan Would Slice EPA Spending by Nearly a Third |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/politics/articles/2017-03-16/trump-budget-proposal-would-slice-epa-spending-by-nearly-a-third |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170425205043/https://www.bloomberg.com/politics/articles/2017-03-16/trump-budget-proposal-would-slice-epa-spending-by-nearly-a-third |archive-date=2017-04-25 |access-date=2017-04-24 |work=Bloomberg.com}}</ref> The proposal drew opposition from environmental and energy-efficiency organizations, as well as businesses.<ref>{{cite news |last=Daly |first=Matthew |date=2017-04-25 |title=Companies decry Trump plan to eliminate Energy Star program |url=https://apnews.com/general-news-united-states-government-5e9411497db94b61a5091892fc96224d |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251121072634/https://apnews.com/general-news-united-states-government-5e9411497db94b61a5091892fc96224d |archive-date=2025-11-21 |access-date=2026-10-11 |work=Associated Press}}</ref> In April 2017, more than 1,000 businesses and organizations signed a letter urging Congress to preserve and strengthen the program.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Thousands of businesses, groups lobby for defense of EPA Energy Star program {{!}} Utility Dive |url=https://www.utilitydive.com/news/thousands-of-businesses-groups-lobby-for-defense-of-epa-energy-star-progra/441409/ |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=www.utilitydive.com |language=en |quote="More than 1,000 businesses and organizations have signed a letter urging Congress to defend and strengthen the Energy Star labeling initiative for efficient appliances that is maintained through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency."}}</ref>

In May 2025, Trump administration officials reportedly announced plans to eliminate Energy Star as part of a broader reorganization of the EPA.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Annie Grayer, Ella Nilsen |date=2025-05-06 |title=Trump admin plans to shut down money-saving Energy Star program soon, sources say {{!}} CNN |url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/05/06/climate/energy-star-trump |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260828023121/https://www.cnn.com/2025/05/06/climate/energy-star-trump |archive-date=2026-08-28 |access-date=2026-10-11 |work=CNN |language=en |quote="The Trump administration is preparing to eliminate two key Environmental Protection Agency divisions focused on climate change and energy efficiency, including its consumer-facing Energy Star program, according to two sources familiar with the plan....The agency is also planning to close its Energy Star program, a longstanding public-private partnership certifying energy efficient appliances and helping consumers find products and tax credits to bring down the cost of energy efficient appliances like air conditioners, heat pumps, refrigerators and washing machines."}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Phillis |first1=Michael |last2=St. John |first2=Alexa |date=2025-05-07 |title=Energy Star, efficiency program that has steered consumer choice, targeted in cuts |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-appliances-consumers-energy-efficiency-3b6100e001a2629dfea9be231f467841 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260218000803/https://apnews.com/article/trump-appliances-consumers-energy-efficiency-3b6100e001a2629dfea9be231f467841 |archive-date=2026-02-18 |access-date=2026-10-11 |work=Associated Press |quote="An Environmental Protection Agency plan to eliminate its Energy Star offices would end a decades-old program that gave consumers a choice to buy environmentally friendly refrigerators, dishwashers and other electronics and save money on electric bills, consumer and environmental groups said. The changes, outlined in agency documents reviewed by The Associated Press, are part of a broad reorganization at the EPA that would eliminate or reorganize significant parts of the office focused on air pollution. Those plans advance President Donald Trump’s sharp turn away from the prior administration’s focus on climate change."}}</ref> The proposal drew opposition from environmental organizations, energy-efficiency advocates, and businesses, which highlighted the program's estimated annual energy cost savings of more than $40 billion compared with approximately $32 million in annual EPA funding.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lavelle |first=By Marianne |date=2025-05-08 |title=As Trump Administration Seeks to Shut Down Energy Star Program, Industry Groups Call to Save It |url=https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08052025/energy-star-program-could-be-eliminated-by-trump-administration/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260406061842/https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08052025/energy-star-program-could-be-eliminated-by-trump-administration/ |archive-date=2026-04-06 |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=Inside Climate News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Lee Zeldin’s Claim that EPA Can Scrap ENERGY STAR Disregards the Law |url=http://www.aceee.org/news/lee-zeldins-claim-epa-can-scrap-energy-star-disregards-law/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261011162918/https://www.aceee.org/news/lee-zeldins-claim-epa-can-scrap-energy-star-disregards-law/ |archive-date=2026-10-11 |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=ACEEE {{!}} American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy |language=en-US |quote="Congress directed the government to run the ENERGY STAR program. In January 2026, Congress enacted bipartisan appropriations legislation providing at least $33 million for Energy Star for fiscal year 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rep. Cole |first=Tom [R-OK-4 |date=2026-01-23 |title=H.R.6938 - 119th Congress (2025-2026): Commerce, Justice, Science; Energy and Water Development; and Interior and Environment Appropriations Act, 2026 |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6938 |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Brady |first=Jeff |date=2026-02-03 |title=Energy Star has emerged stronger after Trump's EPA tried to end it |url=https://www.npr.org/2026/02/03/nx-s1-5684126/energy-star-trump-climate-change |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

In March 2026, the administration announced plans to shift the program from the EPA to the [[United States Department of Energy|DOE]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Energy Star is moving to DOE. Industry groups are hopeful. {{!}} Utility Dive |url=https://www.facilitiesdive.com/news/energy-star-is-moving-to-doe-industry-groups-are-hopeful/814144/ |access-date=2026-03-10 |website=www.facilitiesdive.com |language=en-US}}</ref> A transition plan released on August 28, 2026, outlined the transfer of primary leadership to the DOE with the process targeted for completion by July 2027.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2026-08-28 |title=2026 Status Update |url=https://www.epa.gov/vcs/energy-star |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261010120945/https://www.epa.gov/vcs/energy-star |archive-date=2026-10-10 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/2026-08/ENERGY%20STAR%20Transition%20Plan%20Final%2008.28.2026_508.pdf |title=2026 ENERGY STAR Program Transition Plan |author=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and U.S. Department of Energy |date=2026-08-28 |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |access-date=2026-10-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260901142115/https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/2026-08/ENERGY%20STAR%20Transition%20Plan%20Final%2008.28.2026_508.pdf |archive-date=2026-09-01 |format=PDF |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Specifications==
Energy Star specifications differ with each item and are set by the EPA.

===Computers===
Energy Star 4.0 specifications for computers became effective on July 20, 2007. The requirements are more stringent than the previous specification and existing equipment designs can no longer use the [[service mark]] unless re-qualified. They require the use of [[80 Plus]] Bronze level or higher [[Computer power supply|power supplies]]. Energy Star 5.0 became effective on July 1, 2009.<ref name="DailyTech">Computers with any Energy Star version installed will display its logo, or a [[Rosette (design)|rosette]] and the company's slogan when running the [[BIOS]] after turning the machine on. ({{cite news|url=http://www.dailytech.com/New+Energy+Star+50+Specs+for+Computers+Become+Effective+Today/article15559.htm|title=New Energy Star 5.0 Specs for Computers Become Effective Today|last=Ng|first=Jansen|date=1 July 2009|work=[[DailyTech]]|access-date=2009-07-01|archive-date=2017-06-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170622184250/http://www.dailytech.com/New+Energy+Star+50+Specs+for+Computers+Become+Effective+Today/article15559.htm|url-status=dead}})</ref> Energy Star 6.1 became effective on September 10, 2014. Energy Star 7.1 became effective on November 16, 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/ENERGY%20STAR%20Computers%20Final%20Version%207.1%20Specification_0.pdf|title=Energy Star 7.1 Program Requirements for Computers|access-date=2019-04-25|archive-date=2020-10-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201016231904/https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/ENERGY%20STAR%20Computers%20Final%20Version%207.1%20Specification_0.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> The Version 8.0 specification for computers was finalized on October 15, 2019 and became effective on October 15, 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/ENERGY%20STAR%20Computers%20Final%20Version%208.0%20Specification%20-%20Rev.%20April%202020_0.pdf|title=Energy Star 8.0 Program Requirements for Computers|access-date=2021-01-07|archive-date=2020-12-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202133517/https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/ENERGY%20STAR%20Computers%20Final%20Version%208.0%20Specification%20-%20Rev.%20April%202020_0.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Servers===

The EPA released Version 1.0 of the Computer Server specifications on May 15, 2009. It covered standalone servers with one to four [[CPU socket|processor sockets]]. A second tier to the specification adding active state power and performance reporting for all qualified servers, as well as blade and multi-node server idle state requirements became effective December 16, 2013.<ref>EnergyStar.gov, [https://www.energystar.gov/products/office_equipment/enterprise_servers "Energy Star – Enterprise Servers"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109045158/https://www.energystar.gov/products/office_equipment/enterprise_servers |date=2019-01-09 }}. Retrieved 30 November 2016.</ref> The Version 2.0 Energy Star specification for Computer Servers came into effect on December 16, 2013. The Version 3.0 Energy Star specification for Enterprise Servers came into effect on June 17, 2019 [https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/ENERGY%20STAR%20Version%203.0%20Computer%20Servers%20Program%20Requirements_0.pdf].

===Appliances===
[[File:Dryer EnergyStar4 (15872120794).jpg|thumb|2015 advertisement promoting Energy Star-certified clothes dryers]]
As of early 2008, average [[refrigerators]] need 20% savings over the minimum standard. Dishwashers need at least 41% savings. Most appliances as well as heating and cooling systems have a yellow EnergyGuide label showing the annual cost of operation compared to other models. This label is created through the [[Federal Trade Commission]] and often shows if an appliance is Energy Star rated.<ref>EnergyStar.gov, [http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=appliances.pr_energy_guide "Learn More about EnergyGuide: Energy Star."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210103010005/https://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=appliances.pr_energy_guide |date=2021-01-03 }}. Retrieved 1 March 2008.</ref> While an Energy Star label indicates that the appliance is more energy efficient than the minimum guidelines, purchasing an Energy Star labeled product does not always mean one is getting the most energy efficient option available. For example, dehumidifiers that are rated under {{convert|25|USpt|L}} per day of water extraction receive an Energy Star rating if they have an [[energy factor]] of 1.2 (higher is better), while those rated {{convert|25|USpt|L}} to {{convert|35|USpt|L}} per day receive an Energy Star rating for an energy factor of 1.4 or higher. Thus a higher-capacity but non-Energy Star rated [[dehumidifier]] ''may'' be a more energy efficient alternative than an Energy Star rated but lower-capacity model.<ref name=dehum>Green Energy Efficient Homes, [http://www.green-energy-efficient-homes.com/energy-efficient-dehumidifiers.html Energy Efficient Dehumidifiers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210103041618/https://green-energy-efficient-homes.com/energy-efficient-dehumidifiers.html |date=2021-01-03 }}</ref> The Energy Star program's savings calculator has also been criticized for unrealistic assumptions in its model that tend to magnify savings benefits to the average consumer.<ref>[[Richard Belzer|Belzer, Richard]] ''[http://neutralsource.org/archives/595 Energy Star Appliances: EPA's Savings Calculator Exaggerates Savings] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731002455/http://neutralsource.org/archives/595 | date=2020-07-31}}'', Regulatory Economics, 5 March 2008</ref>

Another factor yet to be considered by the EPA and DOE is the overall effect of energy-saving requirements on the durability and expected service life of a mass-market appliance built to a consumer-level cost standard. For example, a refrigerator may be made more efficient by the use of more insulative spacing and a smaller-capacity compressor using electronics to control operation and temperature. However, this may come at the cost of reduced interior storage (or increased exterior mass) or a reduced service life due to compressor or electronic failures. In particular, electronic controls used on new-generation appliances are subject to damage from shock, vibration, moisture, or power spikes on the electrical circuit to which they are attached. Critics have pointed out that even if a new appliance is energy efficient, any consumer appliance that does not provide [[customer satisfaction]], or must be replaced twice as often as its predecessor contributes to landfill pollution and waste of natural resources used to construct its replacement.<ref>Muñoz, Sara Schaeffer, "Do 'Green' Appliances Live Up To Their Billing", ''The Wall Street Journal'', Business, 2 August 2007</ref>

===Heating and cooling systems===
Energy Star qualified heat pumps, boilers, air conditioning systems, and furnaces are available. In addition, cooling and heating bills can be significantly lowered with air sealing and duct sealing. Air sealing reduces the outdoor air that penetrates a building, and duct sealing prevents attic or basement air from entering ducts and lessening the heating/cooling system’s efficiency. Energy Star qualified [[room air conditioner]]s are at least 10% more energy efficient than the minimum U.S. federal government standards.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=roomac.pr_crit_room_ac | title=Room Air Conditioners Key Product Criteria | publisher=Energystar.gov | access-date=2009-03-23 | archive-date=2015-09-01 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150901051250/http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=roomac.pr_crit_room_ac | url-status=live}}</ref>

===Home electronics===
Energy Star qualified televisions<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://sustainca.org/techshowcase/est/overview | title=California Sustainability Alliance Energy Star Televisions | access-date=2010-07-25 | archive-date=2017-06-27 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170627093453/http://sustainca.org/techshowcase/est/overview | url-status=dead}}</ref> use 30% less energy than average. In November 2008, television specifications were improved to limit on-mode power use, in addition to [[standby power]] which is limited by the current specifications. Standby power consumption for televisions must be 3 watts or less.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia | title=Obstacles to Energy Efficiency | encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Energy | year=2004 | last=Brown | first=Marilyn A. | pages=465–475 | publisher=Elsevier Inc. | doi=10.1016/B0-12-176480-X/00172-8 | isbn=9780121764807 | url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B012176480X001728 | access-date=14 June 2022| url-access=subscription }}</ref>  A wider range of Energy Star qualified televisions will be available.

Other qualified home electronics include cordless phones, battery chargers, VCRs and external power adapters, most of which use 90% less energy.

===Imaging equipment===
The Energy Star Program Requirements for Imaging Products are focused on product families such as electrophotographic (EP) printers, inkjet printers (e.g., thermal), copiers, facsimile machines and other imaging equipment including [[Multi-function printer|MFD]]'s (multifunctional devices). Typical Electrical Consumption (TEC) of a product family are measured and reported against an allowance set by the maximum throughput of the device. Operation modes (OM) are measured and reported for devices such as inkjet products against an allowance set by the functions present in the EUT (equipment under test). Devices that included "adders" such as Ethernet, on-board memory, wireless, etc. are mathematically "added" to increase the OM allowance. On February 1, 2011, the EPA/DOE added the requirement that all products registered under the Energy Star service mark, must be tested by an AB (Accredited Body) or CB (Certification Body) Laboratory.

===Lighting===
[[File:Change Five Lights (13566225195).jpg|thumb|EPA graphic promoting light bulb replacement]]
The Energy Star is awarded to only certain bulbs that meet strict efficiency, quality, and lifetime criteria. Energy Star qualified [[fluorescent lighting]] uses 75% less energy and lasts up to ten times longer than normal [[incandescent light]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/ia/new_homes/features/Lighting_062906.pdf|title=Energy Star Qualified Lighting|website=Energystar.gov|access-date=2 July 2018|archive-date=23 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200723162857/https://www.energystar.gov/ia/new_homes/features/Lighting_062906.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

Energy Star Qualified [[light-emitting diode]] (LED) Lighting:
* Reduces energy costs&nbsp;— uses only 20–25% of the electricity that incandescent bulbs use, and last as much as 25 times as long. LEDs use 25%-30% of the amount of energy as halogen incandescent bulbs, and last 8–25 times as long.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/save-electricity-and-fuel/lighting-choices-save-you-money|title=Lighting Choices to Save You Money {{!}} Department of Energy|website=www.energy.gov|language=en|access-date=2018-07-02|archive-date=2021-01-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210103042650/https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/save-electricity-and-fuel/lighting-choices-save-you-money|url-status=live}}</ref>
* Reduces cooling costs&nbsp;— LEDs produce very little heat.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.earthled.com/blogs/led-lighting-faq-frequently-asked-questions/how-much-heat-is-generated-by-led-light-bulbs|title=How much heat is generated by LED light bulbs?|work=EarthLED.com|access-date=2018-07-02|archive-date=2020-07-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731002536/https://www.earthled.com/blogs/led-lighting-faq-frequently-asked-questions/how-much-heat-is-generated-by-led-light-bulbs|url-status=live}}</ref>

To qualify for Energy Star certification, LED lighting products must pass a variety of tests to prove that the products will display the following characteristics:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/products/lighting_fans/light_bulbs/key_product_criteria|title=Light Bulb Key Product Criteria|website=www.energystar.gov|language=en|access-date=2018-07-02|archive-date=2020-11-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111213527/https://www.energystar.gov/products/lighting_fans/light_bulbs/key_product_criteria|url-status=live}}</ref>
* Brightness is equal to or greater than existing lighting technologies (incandescent or fluorescent) and light is well distributed over the area lighted by the fixture.
* Light output remains constant over time, only decreasing towards the end of the rated lifetime (at least 35,000 hours or 12 years based on use of 8 hours per day).
* Excellent color quality. The shade of white light appears clear and consistent over time.
* Efficiency is as good as or better than fluorescent lighting.
* Light comes on instantly when turned on.
* No flicker when dimmed.
* No off-state power draw. The fixture does not use power when it is turned off, with the exception of external controls, whose power should not exceed 0.5 watts in the off state.

===New Homes===
New homes or apartments that earn the Energy Star label have been verified to meet energy efficiency requirements set by U.S. EPA. Energy Star certified homes are at least 10% more efficient than homes built to code and achieve a 20% improvement on average, while providing homeowners with better quality, performance, and comfort.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/about|title=Energy Star Overview|website=www.energystar.gov|language=en|access-date=2018-08-28|archive-date=2021-01-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210102224156/https://www.energystar.gov/about|url-status=live}}</ref> Nearly 1.9 million Energy Star certified homes and apartments have been certified to date.<ref name="auto"/> These high-performing homes can be found across the U.S. and include a complete thermal enclosure system, a high-efficiency heating, ventilation and cooling system, a comprehensive water management system, and energy-efficient lighting and appliances.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/newhomes/explore_features_benefits|title=Features & Benefits of an Energy Star Certified Home|website=www.energystar.gov|language=en|access-date=2018-08-28|archive-date=2021-01-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210101005009/https://www.energystar.gov/newhomes/explore_features_benefits|url-status=live}}</ref> Together, U.S. homeowners living in certified homes saved $360 million on their energy bills in 2016 alone.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/origins_mission/energy_star_overview/about_energy_star_residential_sector|title=About Energy Star for the Residential Sector|website=www.energystar.gov|language=en|access-date=2018-08-28|archive-date=2020-12-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201214180957/https://www.energystar.gov/about/origins_mission/energy_star_overview/about_energy_star_residential_sector|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2020, Energy Star separated single-family and multifamily construction types into their own programs: Single-Family New Construction (SFNC) and Multifamily New Construction (MFNC).<ref>{{Cite web | title=Policy Record {{!}} ENERGY STAR | url=https://www.energystar.gov/partner_resources/residential_new/program_reqs/policy_record | access-date=June 6, 2022 | website=ENERGY STAR}}</ref>

A new tier of Energy Star certification, called the Energy Star NextGen Certified Homes and Apartments, would be launched in 2023. This new certification uses a baseline of the Energy Star Single-Family and Multifamily certification, with additional requirements such as [[heat pump]] water heaters and EV-ready charging capabilities.<ref>{{Cite web | date=July 16, 2022 | title=Coming in 2023: ENERGY STAR NextGen Certified Homes and Apartments | url=https://www.energystar.gov/newhomeshomes_prog_reqs/energy_star_nextgen | access-date=July 18, 2022 | website=ENERGY STAR}}</ref>

{{Further|Green building in the United States}}

==Energy performance ratings==
The Energy Star program has developed energy performance rating systems for several commercial and institutional building types and manufacturing facilities. These ratings, on a scale of 1 to 100, provide a means for [[benchmarking]] the energy efficiency of specific buildings and industrial plants against the energy performance of similar facilities. The ratings are used by building and energy managers to evaluate the energy performance of existing buildings and industrial plants. The rating systems are also used by EPA to determine if a building or plant can qualify to earn Energy Star recognition.<ref>[http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=evaluate_performance.pt_neprs_learn Energy Star – Evaluate Performance] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110415185124/https://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=evaluate_performance.pt_neprs_learn |date=2011-04-15 }} ''Energy Star.gov''</ref> In 2020 Energy Star released an updated guide for verifying Energy Star certifications.<ref name="ReferenceB">{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/buildings/tools-and-resources/energy-star-guide-licensed-professionals|title=Energy Star Guide for Licensed Professionals|website=www.energystar.gov|access-date=2020-02-23|archive-date=2020-02-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200223233145/https://www.energystar.gov/buildings/tools-and-resources/energy-star-guide-licensed-professionals|url-status=live}}</ref>

Energy Star ratings have been compared to other clean energy rating systems and [[green building certification systems]] such as those by independent firms like [[MIQ Logistics|MiQ]], or [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design|LEED]] certifications for office buildings.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Takahashi|first=Paul|date=2021-09-07|title=Exxon agrees to have some natural gas operations graded on emissions|url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/business/energy/article/Exxon-to-certify-its-natural-gas-production-in-16440836.php|access-date=2021-10-04|website=Houston Chronicle|language=en-US}}</ref>

===Buildings===
[[File:Is your city a true Energy Star? Check out the top 5 cities with the most Energy Star certified buildings. See all 25 winners here- http---go.usa.gov-3r6mH (16902878646).jpg|thumb|2015 graph showing cities with the most Energy Star-certified buildings]]
The number of space types that can receive the energy performance rating in Portfolio Manager is expanding and now includes housing,<ref name="EPA2006">U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, [http://www.energystar.gov/ia/news/downloads/annual_report_2006.pdf "2006 Annual Report: Energy Star and Other Climate Protection Partnerships."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170221050111/https://www.energystar.gov/ia/news/downloads/annual_report_2006.pdf |date=2017-02-21 }}. Retrieved 1 March 2008.</ref> bank/financial institutions, courthouses, hospitals (acute care and children's), hotels and motels, houses of worship, K-12 schools, medical offices, offices, residence halls/dormitories, retail stores, supermarkets, warehouses (refrigerated and non-refrigerated), hotels {{Crossref|text=(see [[hotel energy management]])}}, data centers, senior care facilities, and wastewater facilities.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=eligibility.bus_portfoliomanager_eligibility | title=Criteria for Rating Building Energy Performance | publisher=Energystar.gov | access-date=2009-03-23 | archive-date=2009-05-08 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090508185639/http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=eligibility.bus_portfoliomanager_eligibility | url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="energystar.gov">{{cite web | url=http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=business.bus_bldgs | title=The Energy Star for Buildings & Manufacturing Plants | publisher=Energystar.gov | access-date=2012-12-29 | archive-date=2012-12-30 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121230100420/http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=business.bus_bldgs | url-status=live}}</ref>

Models used in the rating system provide detailed information on the methodologies used to create the energy performance ratings including details on rating objectives, regression techniques, and the steps applied to compute a rating.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=evaluate_performance.bus_portfoliomanager_model_tech_desc | title=Portfolio Manager Overview: Technical Descriptions for Models Used in the Rating System | publisher=Energystar.gov | access-date=2012-12-29 | archive-date=2012-10-31 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121031125155/http://www.energystar.gov/index.cfm?c=evaluate_performance.bus_portfoliomanager_model_tech_desc | url-status=live}}</ref> Energy Star maintains a 1–100 national [[benchmarking]] rating for buildings based on building attributes depending on the category, including [[floor area]], occupancy and energy consumption data into a free online tool provided by Energy Star.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Benchmark Your Building Using ENERGY STAR® Portfolio Manager® | url=https://www.energystar.gov/buildings/benchmark | access-date=2023-12-03 | website=www.energystar.gov | language=en}}</ref>

Energy Star energy performance ratings have been incorporated into some green buildings standards, such as LEED for Existing Buildings. In the U.S., builders of energy efficient homes are able to qualify for Federal Income tax credits and deductions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energystar.gov/about/federal_tax_credits|title=Federal Income Tax Credits and Other Incentives for Energy Efficiency|website=www.energystar.gov|language=en|access-date=2020-02-19|archive-date=2020-02-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200218163604/https://www.energystar.gov/about/federal_tax_credits|url-status=live}}</ref>

Energy Star estimated in 2020 that energy use in commercial buildings accounts for 20% of greenhouse gas emissions, costing more than $100B per year.<ref name="ReferenceB"/>
